## Background

The Internal Audits team have requested a breakdown and analysis of the total spend data available on the IPSA website. This data has been provided year on year since 2010 and contains details of the MP expenses in the areas of office spend, staffing spend, accommodation spend and travel and subsistence spend as well as wind up and start up spend. Total budget information for each category has been made available since 2013.

## Data Characterisation

### Data structure

The Total Spend data consisted of 15 files from the years 2010-11 to 2024-25. Data contents and structure was changeable in some years but 9 columns were consistent across all datasets:

| Column Name                    | Description                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| MP Name                        | Name of MP (Char)                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Constituency                   | Current constituency represented by MP (Char)                                                                                                                                                        |
| PID                            | Personal Unique Identifier of MP (Int)                                                                                                                                                               |
| Office Spend                   | Total spent on office related expenses in financial year (int)                                                                                                                                       |
| Reason for budget set          | Description of why budget was allocated. Where present is either Standard London Area Budget or Standard Non-London Area Budget. Can also contain details of uplifts and reductions from IPSA (char) |
| Remaining office budget        | Amount remaining in office budget at end of financial year (int)                                                                                                                                     |
| Staffing Spend                 | Total spent on staffing related expenses in financial year (int)                                                                                                                                     |
| Remaining Staffing budget      | Amount remaining in staffing budget at end of financial year (int)                                                                                                                                   |
| Accommodation Spend            | Total spent on accommodation related expenses in financial year (int)                                                                                                                                |
| Remaining accommodation budget | Amount remaining in accommodation budget at end of financial year (int)                                                                                                                              |
| Wind up spend                  | Total spent on MP closing affairs upon leaving office (int)                                                                                                                                          |
| Remaining wind up budget       | Amount remaining in wind up budget at end of financial year (int)                                                                                                                                    |

Other columns that were not present in all files included:

-   Subtotals for office spends, 'other parliamentary costs an overall totals

-   'Other costs' spends and budget allocations

-   Office, staffing, accommodation and wind up budgets

-   Travel and subsistence budgets, spends and remaining amounts

-   Previous constituency

The data consisted of 1455 different MPs across 914 constituencies in the United Kingdom. 1111 MPs appear in the data more than once.

### Data Completeness

For the purposes of this and all following analysis, the 15 total spend files were amalgamated into a single master file with one row per MP per year and an overall spend column created which summated the values in the available spend columns for each MP and year.

```{r}
read.csv("\\Data\\Master_Data.csv")
```

Despite being present in all datasets, wind up spend and remaining wind up budget were not fully populated. Probably due the nature of the data contained within, it will only contain information when an MP leaves office which will not happen to every MP every year. In addition to this, gaps in recording were also observed in office spend (6), staffing spend (4), staffing remaining budget (1965, present but not consistently used until 2013/14), accommodation budget (2311, present but not consistently used until 2013/14) and accommodation spend (241)

### General Trends

As staffing, office and accommodation spends were the most consistently used data across all the years of the total spend data, the remainder of the analysis will focus on these columns as well as the calculated overall spend column.

Average overall spends are increasing over time:

```{r}
mean_overall <- master_data %>%
  group_by(Financial.year) %>%
  summarise(avg = mean(Overall.total.spend..calculated.)) %>%
  mutate(years_index = 2010:2024)


mean_overall_bar <- ggplot(mean_overall, aes(x = years_index, y = avg)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",  
    se = FALSE,      
    color = "red",
    size = 1
  ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = mean_overall$years_index,
    labels = mean_overall$years_index
  ) +
  ylab('Average Overall Spend (£)') +
  xlab('Financial Year') +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
    
show(mean_overall_bar)
```

## Z Score Outlier Analysis

In addition to the MPs who had missing data (in years and categories where this was unusual for the data set), an analysis was also performed to detect outliers in terms of amount of spend. This was carried out using Z scores, which calculate the number of standard deviations a value falls from the mean. As the data of interest was roughly normally distributed, Z scores +/- 2 standard deviations from the mean were determined to be outliers (falling within the approximate 5th and 95th percentiles) .

```{r}
hist(master_data$Overall.total.spend..calculated.)
hist(master_data$Office_spend)
hist(master_data$Staffing_spend)
hist(master_data$Accommodation_spend)
```

Plotting individual distributions for each year shows a number of years have bimodal distributions. Typically, one peak is observered towards the bottom end of the spending scale and another towards the middle. This is particularly prevalent in the accommodation spend data, and may represent the difference in claims between MPs who rent accommodation in London versus those own property and claim only utilities related expenses.

```{r}

overall_scatter <- ggplot(master_data, aes(Financial.year, Overall.total.spend..calculated., fill = Financial.year)) +
  geom_violin() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)) +
  ylab('Overall Spend (£)') +
  xlab('Financial Year') 

show(overall_scatter)

office_scatter <- ggplot(master_data, aes(Financial.year, Office_spend, fill = Financial.year)) +
  geom_violin() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)) +
  ylab('Office Spend (£)') +
  xlab('Financial Year') 

show(office_scatter)

staffing_scatter <- ggplot(master_data, aes(Financial.year, Staffing_spend, fill = Financial.year)) +
  geom_violin() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)) +
  ylab('Staffing Spend (£)') +
  xlab('Financial Year') 

show(staffing_scatter)

Accommodation_scatter <- ggplot(master_data, aes(Financial.year, Accommodation_spend, fill = Financial.year)) +
  geom_violin() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)) +
  ylab('Accommodation Spend (£)') +
  xlab('Financial Year') 

show(Accommodation_scatter)

```

As associated costs may differ between MPs whose constituencies are based in London (where rents are higher for office spaces and staffing costs may be higher to account for London weighting) and those note, the z score analysis should control for this and for MPs who own property in London (and claim utilities only), those who rent property in London and those who claim hotel related expenses.

```{r}
#for controlling how much spend MPs are doing, note if their office in London Area or not (office and staffing), they own, rent or use hotels for accomondation in London
constiuencies_in_london <- master_data$Constituency[grep("^Standard London Area budget.*$", master_data$Office_reason.for.budget.set)]
constiuencies_not_in_london <-  master_data$Constituency[grep("^Standard non-London Area budget.*$", master_data$Office_reason.for.budget.set)]

master_data$london_office <- ifelse(master_data$Constituency %in% constiuencies_in_london, 1, 0)

#Note this will only work where I have access to accomodation reason for budget
master_data$accomodation_own_rent_hotel <- 0 #Other/unknown accomoodation status

master_data$accomodation_own_rent_hotel[grep(".*owns.*$", master_data$Accommodation_reason.for.budget.set)] <- 1 #owns their own home in London

master_data$accomodation_own_rent_hotel[grep(".*renting.*$", master_data$Accommodation_reason.for.budget.set)] <- 2 #rents home

master_data$accomodation_own_rent_hotel[grep(".*Hotels.*$", master_data$Accommodation_reason.for.budget.set)] <- 3 #Uses hotels

```

Z score analysis overall

```{r}
master_data <- master_data %>%
  group_by(Financial.year, london_office, accomodation_own_rent_hotel) %>%
  mutate(z_score_overall = (Overall.total.spend..calculated. - mean(Overall.total.spend..calculated.)) / sd(Overall.total.spend..calculated.)) %>%
  ungroup()

over_under_spends <- master_data %>%
  filter(abs(z_score_overall) >= 2) #filter to only those at either "extreme"

overall_overunderspends_plot <- ggplot(over_under_spends, aes(x = Financial.year.factor, y = z_score_overall)) +
  geom_point() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)) +
  ylab('Z Score (Overall Spend)') +
  xlab('Financial Year') 

show(overall_overunderspends_plot)

```

There are substantially more MPs who are spending significantly less than average each financial year than spending more. However, many MPs may be represented more than once.

```{r}
#find those who over or under spend in multiple years 

unique_mps <- unique(over_under_spends$MP.name)

mps_over_under_spending_multiple <- over_under_spends %>%  
  # Keep only relevant categories
  group_by(MP.name) %>%
  summarise(
    num_appearances = n(),                   # Total occurrences
    overspend_count = sum(z_score_overall > 0),     # Count where score > 0
    underspend_count   = sum(z_score_overall < 0),      # Count where score < 0
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(num_appearances))
mps_over_under_spending_multiple

```

Where an MP appears multiple times this is mostly due to repeatedly underspending compared to the average. Although Jim Shannon was found to be spending more than average across 6 years.

```{r}
mps_over_under_spending_multiple %>%
  arrange(desc(overspend_count))
```

To further break this down, the office, accommodation and staffing spends were also analysed to determine if any of these 3 categories were driving over or under spending in MPs.

```{r}
master_data <- master_data %>%
  group_by(Financial.year, london_office) %>%
  mutate(z_score_office = (Office_spend - mean(Office_spend)) / sd(Office_spend)) %>%
  mutate(z_score_staffing = (Staffing_spend - mean(Staffing_spend)) / sd(Staffing_spend)) %>%
  ungroup()

master_data <- master_data %>%
  group_by(Financial.year, accomodation_own_rent_hotel) %>%
  mutate(z_score_accomodation = (Accommodation_spend - mean(Accommodation_spend)) / sd(Accommodation_spend)) %>%
  ungroup()

over_under_spends_office <- master_data %>%
  filter(abs(z_score_office) >= 2)

over_under_spends_staffing <- master_data %>%
  filter(abs(z_score_staffing) >= 2)

over_under_spends_accomodation <- master_data %>%
  filter(abs(z_score_accomodation) >= 2)

over_under_spends_office_plot <- ggplot(over_under_spends_office, aes(x = Financial.year.factor, y = z_score_office)) +
  geom_point() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))

over_under_spends_staffing_plot <- ggplot(over_under_spends_staffing, aes(x = Financial.year.factor, y = z_score_staffing)) +
  geom_point() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))

over_under_spends_accommodation_plot <- ggplot(over_under_spends_accomodation, aes(x = Financial.year.factor, y = z_score_accomodation)) +
  geom_point() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))

show(over_under_spends_office_plot)
show(over_under_spends_staffing_plot)
show(over_under_spends_accommodation_plot)

```

```{r}

mps_over_under_spending_multiple_office <- over_under_spends_office %>%  
  # Keep only relevant categories
  group_by(MP.name) %>%
  summarise(
    num_appearances = n(),                   # Total occurrences
    overspend_count_office = sum(z_score_office > 0),     # Count where score > 0
    underspend_count_office  = sum(z_score_office < 0), # Count where score < 0
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(num_appearances))

mps_over_under_spending_multiple_office


mps_over_under_spending_multiple_office
```

Office and staffing spending follows a similar pattern to the overall spending. Where MPs appear multiple times it is usually in relation to spending below the average rather than above. Ian Blackford over spent the most in his office expenses with 3 separate occurrences. Chuka Umunna and Barry Gardiner both overspent on staffing costs twice in the covered period.

```{r}

mps_over_under_spending_multiple_staffing <- over_under_spends_staffing %>%  
  # Keep only relevant categories
  group_by(MP.name) %>%
  summarise(
    num_appearances = n(),                   # Total occurrences
    overspend_count_staffing = sum(z_score_staffing > 0),     # Count where score > 0
    underspend_count_staffing  = sum(z_score_staffing < 0), # Count where score < 0
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(num_appearances))



```

Accommodation spend followed a different pattern, where the multiple appearances of MPs in the dataset was driven by spending by more than average. Imran Hussain and Jonathan Reynolds both spent more than average on 7 occasions and a further 5 MPs spent more than average on accommodation on 4 or more occasions.

```{r}

mps_over_under_spending_multiple_accommodation <- over_under_spends_accomodation %>%  
  # Keep only relevant categories
  group_by(MP.name) %>%
  summarise(
    num_appearances = n(),                   # Total occurrences
    overspend_count_accommodation = sum(z_score_accomodation > 0),     # Count where score > 0
    underspend_count_accommodation  = sum(z_score_accomodation < 0), # Count where score < 0
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(num_appearances))

mps_over_under_spending_multiple_accommodation

```

### Intrepretation

While significant under spending can be a concern (as it could represent other sources of income which may or may not be declared) it is the recommendation of the report is to focus on those MPs and spending categories where significant over spending is regularly occurring. Jim Shannon was found to be spending more than average in the overall category 6 times, without appearing to spend more than average across the 3 sub categories (office, staffing and accommodation). This could indicate high spending across the 3 sub categories (without being significant) where others with higher spending in one or more categories may have less spending in other categories to balance out their overall spends. It could also indicate higher then average spending in a category not analysed (start up and wind up spend) and this should be analysed in future analysis.

Across the 3 sub categories, only accommodation presented significant numbers (\>3) of repeat appearances by one or more MPs who had spent significantly more than average. after accounting for residential status. This may indicate an area where a review of the accommodation spend policy could be beneficial, to avoid over spending in the future.

## Logistic Regression Modelling

To further explore the relationship between spend categories and whether the constituency was in London (here defined by the proxy of London office location determined by reason for budget set) a logistic regression model was constructed predicting London office status and using office, staffing, accommodation and overall spend as predictors.

```{r}
log_reg_data <- master_data %>% 
  select(MP.name, Office_spend, Staffing_spend, Accommodation_spend, Overall.total.spend..calculated., london_office)


```

In order to meet the assumption of non-co linearity an examination of the correlation between the predictor variables was performed:

```{r}

#check correlations of predictor variables

# Remove the target column
predictors_data <- log_reg_data[, !(names(log_reg_data) %in% c("london_office", "MP.name"))]

#Some NAs are causing problems with the correlation function - remove these for now. Only affects a small number of rows
predictors_data <- na.omit(predictors_data)

# Calculate the correlation matrix
correlation_matrix <- cor(predictors_data)

# Plot the correlation heatmap


melted_corr_matrix <- melt(correlation_matrix)

# Plot the heatmap with ggplot2
ggplot(data = melted_corr_matrix, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", high = "red", mid = "white", 
                       midpoint = 0, limit = c(-1, 1), space = "Lab", 
                       name="Correlation") +
  theme_minimal() + # Minimal theme for a clean look
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "") + # Remove axis labels
  geom_text(aes(Var1, Var2, label = round(value, 2)), color = "black", size = 4) +
  theme(axis.text=element_text(size=15))

```

Overall total spend was highly correlated with both office and staffing spends and so should be omitted from the final model.

```{r}
set.seed(1) #for replicability

#Use 70% of dataset as training set and remaining 30% as testing set


sample <- sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), nrow(log_reg_data), replace=TRUE, prob=c(0.7,0.3))
train <- log_reg_data[sample, ]
test <- log_reg_data[!sample, ]  

#fit model
log_reg_model <- glm(london_office~Office_spend+Staffing_spend+Accommodation_spend, family="binomial", data=train) #omit overall spend as it will be correlated to the other 3


#view model summary
summary(log_reg_model)
```

All three predictors were significantly predictive of office location, with both unit increases in office and staffing spend associated with average increase in the log odds of the office location being in London of .000022 and .0000071 respectively. Accommodation spend was negatively predictive of London office location, with a unit increase in accommodation spend resulting in a decrease in the log odds of the office being in London of -.00063. MPs who represent London constituencies seem to spend more on office spends and staffing spends, but less on accommodation (perhaps because they own property in the area already and so claim fewer expenses).

The predictive performance of the model, as show by McFaddens R2 was relatively good.

```{r}
pscl::pR2(log_reg_model)["McFadden"] #.47 is quite good for McFadden
```

Testing the model further with sensitivty and specificity analysis indicated the model is better at avoiding false positives i.e. mislabelling non-London offices as London offices then it is at labelling London offices correctly.

```{r}

#predict the test set and see where it differs from 'reality'

test$office_loc_predict <- predict(log_reg_model, test, type="response")

test$london_office_prediction <- ifelse(test$office_loc_predict >= 0.5, 1, 0)

xtabs(~ london_office + london_office_prediction, data = test)


#Sensitivity and specificity analysis

sensitivity_london_office <- 268/(268+193) 

specificity_london_office <- 2592/(2592 + 113)

print(paste("Sensitivity:", sensitivity_london_office))
print(paste("Specificity:", specificity_london_office))
```

The model could also be used as a form of outlier analysis, using spend data to predict an MPs office location. Where this was assigned to be London where it is not, this could indicate over spending in the MPs accounts, or if happening across a number of MPs, it could be taken as evidence of a needed adjustment to the allocated spends of MPs in other parts of the country.

## Future Work

The current analysis was limited in the variables examined, only analysing the variables that were most well populated and common across all the datasets. Future analysis should complete the analysis and include the variables not analysed, with adjustments made for the missing data present across some of the years in these variables. Further, the analysis did not take into account additional information regarding the MPs budgets. This was not available for all years, but future analysis could take into account the allocated budgets of MPs in the years where this data is available and calculate a proportion of the budget used by MPs. It should also incorporate additional information regarding additional funds allocated by IPSA to individuals - for example following an uplift application or carried forwards from previous years. Further modelling could ask if past over/underspending in MPs is predictive of future over/under spending and attempting to understand this relationship further.
